Estimating prevalence

Source: vignettes/articles/tutorial-prevalence.Rmd
tutorial-prevalence.Rmd
library(MMSpower)

A national malaria programme wants to know how common a drug-resistance marker (say, a validated kelch13 mutation) is in one region. Earlier reports suggest about 20% of infections carry it, and the programme wants to estimate the prevalence to within ±5 percentage points, with 95% confidence.

Two functions do the work: design_precision() says how many samples to collect, and estimate_prevalence() analyses them once they are in.

Part 1: Designing the study

How many samples, ignoring clustering?

Start with the simplest case: every sample is independent (as if drawn by simple random sampling across the region) and the test is perfect.

d0 <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05)
d0
#> $n
#> [1] 264
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 264
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04996977

So 264 samples are needed. By default design_precision() sizes the study for a Clopper-Pearson interval, the same default as estimate_prevalence(), so the analysis gives back the margin of error that was planned. There is no formula for this, so the function finds the sample size by a numerical search. The familiar z2p(1−p)/MOE2z^2 p(1-p) / \text{MOE}^2 formula, rounded up, is the Wald version, which you get with ci_method = "wald":

design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, ci_method = "wald")$n
#> [1] 246

This is the number most textbooks and the MMS-SD workshop give. The Clopper-Pearson interval is a little wider, so it needs a few more samples. The result also gives moe, the margin of error the rounded design actually achieves, here 0.04997, just inside the target. Two things drive it: the margin of error (halving it roughly quadruples the sample size) and the expected prevalence (the sample size is largest at 50%). If the expected prevalence is uncertain, using a value closer to 50% is the cautious choice.

An imperfect test

Molecular assays are good but not perfect. Suppose the assay has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%: it misses some true positives, and some negatives are wrongly called positive.

d_test <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05,
                           sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
d_test$n
#> [1] 387

The sample size rises from 264 to 387. The reason is that the analysis will correct the measured prevalence back to the true scale (the Rogan-Gladen correction), and this correction stretches the confidence interval by a factor of 1/(Se+Sp−1)1 / (Se + Sp - 1). To keep the same margin of error on the true scale, more samples are needed. Specificity matters more than its size suggests: at low prevalence, false positives can make up a large share of the positives.

Clustering: samples come from sites

In practice samples are collected at a number of sites (health facilities, villages), not drawn at random from the whole region. People at the same site tend to be more alike than people at different sites, so each extra sample from a site adds less information than a sample from a new site. The intra-cluster correlation (ICC) measures how strong this is, and the design effect Deff=1+(npersite−1)ICCD_{eff} = 1 + (n_{per\,site} - 1)\,\text{ICC} says how much the sample size has to grow. For this tutorial we assume an ICC of 0.05, and go back to a perfect test to keep the numbers simple.

There are two ways to fix the design, depending on what is constrained in the field.

Fixing people per site. If each site can realistically collect 20 samples, solve for the number of sites:

d_per <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
#> $n
#> [1] 520
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 26
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.95
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 264
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04971169

The study needs 26 sites of 20 people, 520 samples in total.

Fixing the number of sites. If the programme already has 20 sentinel sites, solve for the number of people per site:

d_sites <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
#> $n
#> [1] 740
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 20
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 37
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 2.8
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 264
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04994193

Each of the 20 sites now needs 37 people, 740 samples in total.

In both cases n_eff is the unclustered answer from the first section: the clustered design carries the same information as 264 independent samples. Fixing the sites at 20 needs more samples in total than fixing 20 people per site, because the people per site go up, and so does the design effect.

Too few sites. With the number of sites fixed, there is a limit. Each site is worth at most 1/ICC1 / \text{ICC} independent samples, however many people are tested there, so a small number of sites can never reach the target precision:

design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 10, icc = 0.05)
#> Error:
#> ! Target MOE of 5.0% is unachievable with 10 sites and ICC = 0.050; the minimum achievable MOE is 5.8%.

The error reports the best margin of error that 10 sites can give. The options are to add sites, accept a wider margin of error, or (if there is evidence for it) assume a smaller ICC.

More sites, fewer samples

The same precision can be reached with many different numbers of sites, and spreading the samples over more sites reduces the total needed:

design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 15, icc = 0.05)$n
#> [1] 2070
design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 30, icc = 0.05)$n
#> [1] 450
design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 100, icc = 0.05)$n
#> [1] 300

With 15 sites the study needs 2070 samples; with 100 sites, only 300, close to the 264 an unclustered survey would need. Each new site brings in fresh information, whereas each extra sample at a site partly repeats what that site has already shown. So, where the budget and logistics allow, aim for more sites with fewer people at each. Site visits cost money too, and the Costing a study tutorial shows how to find the cheapest design.

The precision of a design you already have

Sometimes the design is set by circumstances: a network of sentinel sites that can each collect a fixed number of samples, say. Give the full design and leave out moe, and design_precision() returns the margin of error that design achieves:

d_have <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, n_sites = 20, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_have$moe
#> [1] 0.0569166

Twenty sites of 20 people give a margin of error of ±5.7 percentage points, a little wider than the 5-point target.

Sites do not have to be the same size. Give n_per_site as one value per site:

d_uneven <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, n_per_site = c(250, 250, 60, 60, 40, 40),
                             icc = 0.05)
d_uneven$moe
#> [1] 0.1025958

d_even <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, n_sites = 6, n_per_site = 117, icc = 0.05)
d_even$moe
#> [1] 0.08123823

These six sites hold 700 people and give a margin of error of ±10.3 points. Spreading about the same number evenly, 6 sites of 117, gives ±8.1. Large sites dominate the estimate, and many of their people repeat what that site has already shown, so uneven site sizes cost precision.

Allowing for dropout and suspected cases

The design functions give the number of samples needed at analysis. More people than that have to be enrolled, for two reasons.

First, some samples are lost: consent is withdrawn, a sample is lost in transit, or the assay fails. If about 10% are expected to be lost, divide by 1−0.11 - 0.1 and round up. Do this per site, not only for the total, so that every site still delivers its share. Taking the design with 20 samples at each of 26 sites:

per_site_analysis  <- d_per$n_per_site
per_site_confirmed <- ceiling(per_site_analysis / (1 - 0.1))
per_site_confirmed
#> [1] 23

Second, the marker is measured only in confirmed P. falciparum infections, but people are enrolled as suspected cases, before the test result is known. If about 40% of suspected cases are confirmed, divide again by 0.4:

per_site_suspected <- ceiling(per_site_confirmed / 0.4)
per_site_suspected
#> [1] 58

So each site enrols 58 suspected cases, expecting 23 of them to be confirmed, and 20 samples to reach the analysis. Across the 26 sites that is 1508 suspected cases enrolled, 598 confirmed cases enrolled and 520 samples expected at analysis. Keep the three numbers apart when planning and reporting: the design was calculated for the last one.

The confirmed fraction often differs between sites, for example with transmission intensity. Use each site’s own value:

ceiling(per_site_confirmed / c(0.6, 0.4, 0.25))
#> [1] 39 58 92

A site where only a quarter of suspected cases are confirmed has to enrol 92 suspected cases to deliver the same 20 samples. When budgeting, cost the inflated numbers, since those are the people enrolled and tested: in estimate_cost(), the suspected cases are n_screened, the confirmed cases n_collected and the samples at analysis n_sequenced (see Costing a study).

Part 2: Analysing the data

Suppose the programme settles on 20 sites of about 30 people, and records the number of samples carrying the marker (x) and the number tested (n) at each site:

x <- c(4, 9, 6, 2, 11, 7, 5, 8, 3, 6, 10, 4, 7, 5, 12, 6, 3, 8, 5, 7)
n <- c(30, 32, 28, 31, 30, 29, 33, 30, 27, 31, 30, 32, 29, 30, 31, 28, 30, 30, 32, 29)

The estimate

By default the ICC is estimated from the spread of the site prevalences, and an exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval is returned:

est <- estimate_prevalence(x, n)
est
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.2126246
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.172139
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 0.2577502
#> 
#> $moe
#> [1] 0.04280562
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 424.3709
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0.01434799
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.41857
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] 19

The estimated prevalence is 21.3%, with a 95% interval from 17.2% to 25.8%. deff is the design effect worked out from the estimated ICC, and n_eff is the number of independent samples the clustered data are worth. df is the number of sites minus one: the ICC was estimated from 20 sites, and the interval is widened a little to allow for the uncertainty in that estimate (see below).

Choosing an interval method

Three interval methods are available. They give the same point estimate but different intervals:

cp <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "clopper-pearson")
c(cp$ci_lower, cp$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1721390 0.2577502

wald <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "wald")
c(wald$ci_lower, wald$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1710528 0.2541964

ac <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "agresti-coull")
c(ac$ci_lower, ac$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1739951 0.2571266

With this much data and a prevalence well away from 0 they are close. The differences matter for small samples or a prevalence near 0 or 1. There the Wald interval is too narrow, has zero width when no positives are seen, and its limits can fall below 0 or above 1. estimate_prevalence() sets such limits to 0 or 1, which keeps the interval sensible, but the result is still less reliable than the other two methods in these situations. Clopper-Pearson, the default, is the cautious choice, and Agresti-Coull a good compromise. Use the same method at both stages: design_precision() takes the same ci_method argument, so a study sized for Clopper-Pearson (the default in both) gives back the planned margin of error when analysed with it. See ?estimate_prevalence for the details.

Supplied or estimated ICC?

The interval depends on the ICC, and estimating an ICC needs data from many sites: with only a handful, the estimate is unreliable. estimate_prevalence() allows for this by widening the interval according to the number of sites the ICC was estimated from. With many sites this makes little difference, but with a handful the interval becomes very wide. So with few sites it is often better to supply a cautious value, for example from earlier surveys in similar settings:

est_icc <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, icc = 0.05)
c(est_icc$ci_lower, est_icc$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1630936 0.2692575

With 20 sites the estimate is usable: it gave an ICC of 0.014 and an interval from 17.2% to 25.8%, while supplying 0.05 gives 16.3% to 26.9%. The clustering concepts article shows how variable ICC estimates are with few sites.

An imperfect test at analysis

If the assay is imperfect, give its sensitivity and specificity, and the estimate and interval are corrected to the true-prevalence scale:

est_test <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
c(est_test$prevalence, est_test$ci_lower, est_test$ci_upper)
#> [1] 0.1913230 0.1436929 0.2444121

The corrected prevalence is lower than the measured one, because at this prevalence false positives outnumber missed cases, and the interval is wider. The sensitivity and specificity given here should be the same values assumed when the study was designed: the design only delivers the planned margin of error if the analysis makes the same correction.
